definition: To obscure, render unclear, or complicate language in a way that conceals methodological details or weak findings.
etymology: From Late Latin obfuscatus, past participle of obfuscare ('to darken').
manuscriptExample: Passive voice constructions in the results section serve only to obfuscate the sequence of enzyme digestion steps.
conferenceExample: We asked the authors to revise Figure 3 because crowded axes obfuscate statistical differences between wild-type and mutant lineages.

definition: Stated or appearing to be true or present, but not necessarily confirmed upon rigorous mechanistic inspection.
etymology: From French ostensible, from Latin ostensus ('shown').
manuscriptExample: The ostensible increase in proliferation was shown to stem from vehicle evaporation in outer microplate wells.
conferenceExample: Reviewer 1 pointed out that the ostensible drug selectivity vanished when tested against isoform variants.

definition: Statistically independent or utilizing completely distinct physical/chemical methods to validate a hypothesis.
manuscriptExample: To confirm flow cytometry results, we employed an orthogonal assay based on single-molecule mass photometry.
conferenceExample: The referee strongly urged the authors to provide orthogonal evidence before claiming direct receptor activation.
